task: What does a valid WebMCP Challenge submission have to include? List all deliverables and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository.
answer: A valid submission must include four deliverables: (1) a working live URL that judges can access with ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled; (2) a text description explaining why the use case strongly fits WebMCP, how it improves the user experience, what people and agents can do together that was previously difficult or impossible, and briefly how WebMCP was implemented; (3) a public YouTube demo video under three minutes, with audio, clearly showing what was built and how WebMCP was used; and (4) a URL to a public GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repository. The repository must contain all source code, assets, and instructions needed for the project to function, and it must be open source with a license file that is detectable and visible at the top of the repository page in the About section.

task: Can a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualify? Explain which work counts, how judges assess it, and what evidence the entrant must provide.
answer: Yes. A project that existed before the August 25, 2026 Submission Period start can qualify only if it was meaningfully extended with WebMCP after that start date. Judges evaluate a pre-existing project solely on the work added during the Submission Period, not on its earlier functionality. The entrant must clearly distinguish old work from new work and document that the WebMCP extension was made within the Submission Period, using timestamped or dated commit history, or equivalent evidence.

task: Give the final extended submission deadline in PT and in EDT. Explain why it changed and identify the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close.
answer: The final extended deadline is Friday, September 4, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. PT, which is 4:00 a.m. EDT. It moved by 12 hours because an ongoing outage was affecting entrants while the OpenAI team worked on a fix. After submissions close, the repository, demo video, and live site/application must remain unchanged: do not edit the repo, replace the video, alter the live site, or take the site offline. The official rules also state more generally that the submitted entry may no longer be changed, even though the separate Devpost portfolio project may continue to be updated.

task: How do the two judging stages work? Name all four equally weighted criteria in the second stage and explain the tie-breaking order.
answer: Stage One is a pass/fail viability screen: the project must reasonably fit the challenge theme and reasonably apply the required APIs/SDKs. Every submission that passes advances to Stage Two, where judges score four equally weighted criteria: WebMCP Leverage (depth, skill, genuine effort, and a working non-trivial WebMCP implementation); Execution (a working/runnable, complete and coherent product experience rather than merely a technical proof of concept); Potential Impact (a credible, specific real problem and audience that the demonstrated solution actually addresses); and Creativity & Ambition (novelty, creativity, and differentiation from existing concepts). Highest overall scores determine potential winners. For a tie, compare the tied entries on the first listed applicable criterion, WebMCP Leverage; if still tied, proceed in listed order through Execution, Potential Impact, then Creativity & Ambition. If they remain tied across every applicable criterion, the judges vote.

task: How can judges test a submitted application in each supported browser environment? Include the minimum Chrome version and required flag, whether judges must open the live application, and where an entrant must provide private login credentials.
answer: Entrants must provide a working live URL. Judges can open it in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, where WebMCP works out of the box, or in Google Chrome 149 or later after enabling the experimental flag at chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Judges are allowed to test the live application but are not required to open it: they may judge from the text description, images, and demo video alone, so those materials and the README should stand on their own. The live project should remain free and unrestricted for testing through the end of judging. If authentication is necessary, the entrant must put the login credentials in the private Testing Instructions field of the submission form; only Devpost managers and judges can see it.
